Where is Linn County, Iowa, and what towns does it include?

Linn County sits in eastern Iowa, with Cedar Rapids as both its county seat and its largest city. The county was created on December 21, 1837, as part of Wisconsin Territory, and the seat moved from Marion to Cedar Rapids after voters approved the change in 1919 (Wikipedia).

It covers 724.669 square miles, which makes it the tenth largest county in Iowa by area. Its neighbors are Benton, Buchanan, Cedar, Delaware, Iowa, Johnson and Jones counties. The 2020 census counted 230,299 residents, the second-highest total of any Iowa county.

A seller's first practical question is which assessor and which school or city services apply, and the answer can change from one side of a city line to the other.

What drives the Linn County economy?

Cedar Rapids anchors the county's economy, with aerospace, grain processing and trucking among its large employers. A 2024 city report, as summarized on Wikipedia, ranks Collins Aerospace in the 5,000 to 9,999 employee range.

  • Employers in the 1,000 to 4,999 range include Aegon USA, the Cedar Rapids Community School District, the City of Cedar Rapids, Cedar Rapids Steel Transport, Kirkwood Community College, PepsiCo and UnityPoint Health-St. Luke's.
  • Grain processing directly provides about 4,000 jobs in the city, and a large Quaker Oats mill sits on the north side of downtown.
  • CRST, a trucking company, is based in Cedar Rapids, and Aegon has its U.S. headquarters there.
  • In February 2025 a $750 million data center by Quality Technology Services was announced.

Coe College and Mount Mercy University are the city's four-year colleges, and Kirkwood Community College is the area's two-year college.

How did the 2008 flood and 2020 derecho affect Linn County homes?

Both events left lasting marks on Cedar Rapids housing. The Cedar River reached a record 31.12 feet on June 13, 2008, and 1,126 city blocks flooded, with 561 blocks severely damaged. About 7,749 properties were evacuated, including 5,900 homes, and at least 1,300 properties had to be demolished.

On August 10, 2020, a derecho hit the county with sustained winds of 60 to 80 miles per hour and gusts of 110 or more. Most residential and commercial buildings in Cedar Rapids were damaged, along with 20 schools, and about 95 percent of the city lost power.

For a seller, that history means older Cedar Rapids houses may carry past repair work. Gathering permits, contractor invoices and insurance paperwork before you talk to a buyer saves time, and a cash buyer who purchases as-is can take a house in its current condition.

Which office handles Linn County property assessments?

It depends on where the house is. The Linn County Assessor covers the county's real property, and Cedar Rapids has its own City Assessor. The table lists the offices a Linn County seller is most likely to contact.

OfficeRoleContact
Linn County AssessorValues real property; revalues every two years on odd-numbered years; assessment date January 1linn.iowaassessors.com
Cedar Rapids City AssessorValues property in Cedar Rapids; revalued every year500 15th Avenue SW, 319-286-5888
Linn County TreasurerCollects tax, runs the tax sale, handles redemptions935 Second St. SW, 319-892-5500
Board of ReviewHears assessment protests; five members appointed by the Conference BoardThrough the assessor's office

Neither assessor collects tax or sets the rate. The City Assessor's page says its office "does not collect taxes, calculate taxes nor determine tax rate," and the county assessor's page puts the focus on value, with taxing bodies setting budgets and levies. Public utilities and railroads are assessed by the Iowa Department of Revenue.

What is the Linn County property tax calendar?

Assessment is as of January 1, bills are paid in two halves, and protests are due in April. The Linn County Assessor's timeline and the statewide treasurers' calendar line up as follows.

DateEvent
January 1Assessment date
By April 1Assessors complete assessments and notify owners
April 2 to 25Informal assessor hearings can be requested
April 2 to 30Protests filed with the Board of Review
May 1 to 31Board of Review considers protests
October 1Final equalization orders issued
October 9 to 31Equalization protests to the board
September 30 and March 31First and second halves payable
Third Monday in JuneAnnual county tax sale of unpaid parcels

The Linn County Treasurer says spring payments must be postmarked by March 31 and fall payments by September 30. Delinquent installments carry interest of 1.5 percent per month.

How do I protest a Linn County assessment?

File a written protest with the Board of Review between April 2 and April 30 of the assessment year. The board cannot extend that deadline, except in a declared disaster area, where the filing period runs May 1 through June 5 (Iowa Code 441.37).

The statute allows five grounds:

  • The assessment is not equitable compared with like property in the taxing district.
  • The property is assessed for more than the value the law allows.
  • The property is not assessable, is exempt, or is misclassified.
  • There is an error in the assessment.
  • There is fraud or misconduct, which must be stated specifically.

An oral hearing is available only if you request it in writing when you file. One form can cover several parcels if the same grounds apply. After deciding, the board must send written notice of its action and the reasons.

How do I pay Linn County property tax?

You can pay online, by mail, in a drop box, by phone or in person at the Treasurer's office at 935 Second St. SW in Cedar Rapids. Checks go to the Linn County Treasurer, and the tax statement stub should go with the payment so it is credited correctly.

  • In-person cash and check payments carry no fee.
  • Online check payments cost $0.30, debit cards cost $3.25 plus $0.30 per transaction, and credit cards cost 2.20 percent plus $0.30 per transaction.
  • Online cash payments are not accepted.
  • Lobby hours are Monday through Friday, 7:30 a.m. to 4 p.m., with extended hours of 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. on the second Wednesday of each month.

The Treasurer warns that USPS now postmarks mail by the day it is processed, not the day it is dropped off, so a late-processed envelope can be treated as late. A free manual postmark from a staffed retail counter avoids that.

What happens to Linn County property tax when I sell?

The tax stays with the property, so a sale has to account for any unpaid installments at closing. A closing agent splits the current installment under the purchase contract, and any delinquent amount is paid from proceeds so the buyer receives a clean title.

The Treasurer's office also prepares plat and mobile home clearances and processes tax suspensions, which can matter at closing. Iowa's transfer tax is 80 cents for each $500 of value above the first $500, and the seller, as grantor, is the person liable (Iowa Code 428A.1 and 428A.3).

If taxes are far behind, the county can sell them at the June tax sale. The Treasurer conducts the sale, processes redemptions and issues tax sale deeds, and redemption of a sold parcel costs the sold amount plus 2 percent interest per month. Our statewide Iowa tax deed and tax lien sales guide covers the redemption steps. More questions about Linn County, IA Property Tax Guide

Who assesses property in Cedar Rapids?

The Cedar Rapids City Assessor does, from the City Services Center at 500 15th Avenue SW. The Linn County Assessor covers the rest of the county's real property.

When are Linn County property taxes due?

The first half is due September 1 and payable through September 30, and the second half is due March 1 and payable through March 31. Payments must be postmarked by those dates.

What is the deadline to protest a Linn County assessment?

April 30 of the assessment year, with filing opening April 2. Declared disaster areas get May 1 through June 5.

What late interest applies in Linn County?

Delinquent installments accrue interest of 1.5 percent per month, and the Treasurer notes a 1.5 percent late fee when a payment arrives without a valid postmark.

Where do I call the Linn County Treasurer?

319-892-5500, Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Phone hold times may be long, so a visit or an appointment at the Public Service Center can be faster.

Where is Scott County, Iowa, and which towns does it include?

Scott County sits on the Mississippi River in eastern Iowa and is part of the Quad Cities metro area. Davenport is both the county seat and the largest city.

The county covers about 468 square miles, of which roughly 458 are land. Across the river lies Rock Island County, Illinois. To the north is Clinton County, to the northwest Cedar County, and to the southwest Muscatine County. Part of the Upper Mississippi River National Wildlife and Fish Refuge falls inside the county line.

The 2020 census counts for the larger communities are below. Each one sits in a different school and city-service area, which is why the same county tax bill can look quite different from one address to the next.

Source for the list and the land area: the Scott County entry on Wikipedia.

How did Scott County begin?

The Wisconsin territorial legislature created Scott County on December 21, 1837. It was named for General Winfield Scott, who presided over the signing of the treaty that ended the Black Hawk War.

The first American settlement was Clark's Ferry, also called Clark's Landing, which is now the town of Buffalo. It dates to 1833. The river made the area a crossing point from the start.

Two colleges anchor the county: Saint Ambrose University in Davenport and Scott Community College in Riverdale.

Who assesses property in Scott County?

Two assessors share the county. The Scott County Assessor covers everything except the City of Davenport, and Davenport has its own City Assessor.

Both offices are on the fifth floor of the Scott County Administrative Center in Davenport. The county's records search lets you look up assessor, auditor and treasurer records by name, address or parcel number, and Davenport City Assessor records are included in that search.

This split is the first thing to sort out if you own a house here. A home in Bettendorf, Eldridge or a rural township goes through the county assessor. A home inside Davenport goes through the city assessor. Check the parcel record before you call anyone, so you reach the right office on the first try.

Iowa sets the formal protest window for assessments in state law. The existing guidance on this page lists the Board of Review window as April 2 through April 30 under Iowa Code 441.37. Ask the assessor that covers your parcel how to file and whether an informal review is available first.

When is Scott County property tax due, and how can you pay it?

Scott County collects property tax in two equal installments, due September 30 and March 31 of the following year. When a due date lands on a weekend or holiday, it moves to the next business day.

Taxes are certified in July or August. Interest starts on the first business day after each due date, so a payment that arrives one day late is already delinquent. The Treasurer's page does not list the interest rate, so ask the office for the current figure before you calculate a payoff.

Payment options and fees listed by the Treasurer:

MethodWhereFee
CashCounter onlyNone
CheckCounter, mail, drop boxNone at the counter
E-checkOnline$0.25

Debit cardCounter only$2.00 per transaction

The Treasurer has two offices: the Scott County Administrative Center at 600 W. 4th St. in Davenport, and the Scott County General Store at 902 W. Kimberly Rd., Suite 6D, in Davenport. Mailed payments go to 600 W 4th St, Davenport, IA 52801-1003. Both locations have a drop box for checks, and the Treasurer gives preference to visitors with an appointment.

What happens when Scott County property tax goes unpaid?

Delinquent taxes are published in June and sold at the annual tax sale, held on the third Monday of June. The buyer receives a certificate.

If nobody buys the taxes after two publications, the certificate goes to Scott County. If the taxes are not redeemed within the set period, the certificate holder can receive a deed, and county-held properties are usually auctioned.

For an owner who is behind, the timeline matters more than any single number:

  • September 30 and March 31 are the dates interest can begin the next business day.
  • June is when delinquent parcels are published.
  • The third Monday of June is the sale date.
  • Redemption is possible until the period set by law runs out.

Selling before the sale date is one way to clear the lien from the title. A buyer who pays cash can often close fast enough to pay the county out of the proceeds, but you should confirm the exact payoff amount with the Treasurer first.

What do you need to record a deed in Scott County?

The Scott County Recorder will refuse a deed unless it includes the required statements and blocks. The Recorder's page lists several items that sellers and closing agents often forget.

  • A Declaration of Value statement, required for deeds, contracts, assignments of contracts and quit claim deeds unless the document is exempt.
  • Revenue (transfer) tax on the full sale price over $500, or a stated exemption on the face of the document under Iowa Code chapter 428A.2.
  • A groundwater hazard statement, or the sentence that the transaction is exempt from the requirement. Since July 1, 2022, sellers may skip the statement if none of the listed conditions exist on the property.
  • A Prepared by block with name, address and telephone, and an Address tax statement block with name, address and zip code, placed below the required blank space at the top of the page.
  • A complete legal description.

The property owner is responsible for the accuracy of the groundwater statement. The Recorder points sellers to a realtor or an attorney for questions, and the form itself is posted by the Iowa Department of Natural Resources.

How does a cash sale work when taxes are due in Scott County?

A cash sale in Scott County follows the same title steps as any other sale, but it skips the lender and the appraisal. That removes two common sources of delay.

Before closing, the closing agent checks the Treasurer record for unpaid installments and any tax sale certificate. If the first installment is open, it is paid from the sale proceeds. If a certificate has been issued, the holder has to be paid and released before the deed can clear.

Sellers in Scott County commonly run into these situations:

  • An inherited house in Davenport with the last installment unpaid and no one living there.
  • A rental in a river-town neighborhood with deferred repairs that make a bank appraisal difficult.
  • A house split between two heirs who live in different states and cannot agree on repairs.

If any of these describe your property, send us the address and a brief note about the tax status. We will tell you whether the parcel is in the county or the Davenport assessment system and what we need to see before we write an offer.

Who sends the property tax bill in Scott County?

The Scott County Treasurer collects property tax for the county, cities, schools and other taxing bodies. Assessments come from the Scott County Assessor, or from the Davenport City Assessor if the house is inside Davenport.

What are the Scott County property tax due dates?

The first installment is due September 30 and the second is due March 31 of the following year. If the date falls on a weekend or holiday, it moves to the next business day.

Can I pay Scott County property tax online?

Yes. The Treasurer accepts e-checks and credit cards online. The e-check fee is $0.25 and the credit card fee is 2.25%. Cash and debit cards are not accepted online.

When is the Scott County tax sale?

The annual tax sale is held on the third Monday of June. Delinquent taxes are published in June before that date.

Which Scott County office handles assessment questions inside Davenport?

The Davenport City Assessor, located with the county offices on the fifth floor of the Scott County Administrative Center. The Scott County Assessor covers the rest of the county.

Can I sell a Scott County house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. Unpaid taxes are paid from the sale proceeds at closing. Get a current payoff from the Treasurer before you accept any offer so you know how much will be deducted.

Where is Dallas County, Iowa?

Dallas County is in central Iowa, directly west of Des Moines, and it is part of the Des Moines to West Des Moines metropolitan area. It covers about 592 square miles, which ranks 24th among Iowa counties by area, and Adel is the county seat.

Its neighbors are Polk to the east, Boone and Greene to the north, Guthrie and Adair to the west and southwest, and Madison and Warren to the south and southeast.

Cities in the county include Waukee (the largest), Urbandale, Clive, Grimes, Perry, Adel, Granger, Dallas Center, Van Meter, Woodward, De Soto, Redfield, Dexter and Minburn. West Des Moines is mostly in Polk County, so a West Des Moines address can be billed by either county, and the parcel record settles which.

How fast has Dallas County grown?

Dallas County was the fastest growing county in Iowa from 2010 to 2020, and the Census Bureau called it the fastest growing in the Midwest from July 2020 to July 2025. It is now the sixth most populous county in Iowa.

YearDallas County population

Waukee alone went from 5,126 residents in 2000 to 23,940 in 2020.

How did Dallas County get started?

The Sac and Fox nation ceded this land under an 1842 treaty, and the Iowa Territory's legislature created Dallas County on January 13, 1846. It is named for George M. Dallas, vice president under James K. Polk.

Adel is the oldest town in the county and sits on the North Raccoon River, where a flour mill built in 1856 and 1857 used the water power. The Dallas County Courthouse there was finished in 1902 and stands in the middle of downtown. The railroad line along the river is now the Raccoon River Valley Trail.

Perry and Waukee were both laid out as towns in 1869. Waukee is likely named after the Milwaukee Road railroad.

What do the Census Bureau figures show for Dallas County housing?

For 2020 to 2024, the Census Bureau reports a median value of owner-occupied homes of $355,600 in Dallas County and an owner-occupied rate of 69.0 percent. Median household income was $102,379.

  • Housing units, July 2025: 49,625
  • Persons per household: 2.53
  • Bachelor's degree or higher, age 25+: 51.5%
  • Waukee median household income (2023 survey): $106,728
  • Adel median age (2020): 35.3, with about 30% of residents under 18

These are county wide estimates, not figures for any single town.

What shapes the local economy and getting around?

Dallas County's economy is tied to the Des Moines metropolitan area, with Interstate 80, US 6 and US 169 and Iowa Highways 17, 44, 141, 144 and 210 crossing the county.

Apple chose Waukee in 2017 for a $1.38 billion data center campus, and the Waukee Community School District serves more than 13,600 students from Clive, Urbandale, Waukee and West Des Moines. Waukee has no fixed route transit, and the Des Moines Area Regional Transit route 92 runs in Clive, about half a mile away.

Adel is the base of Stine Seed. Perry went the other direction: the Tyson pork plant, its main employer, closed in June 2024 and eliminated an estimated 1,300 jobs, about 800 held by Perry residents.

Which Dallas County offices handle property tax?

Most county property offices are in the Administration Building at 800 Court Street in Adel, with a second county location in Perry. The county directory lists the courthouse at 801 Court Street.

  • Treasurer, Tax Division: 800 Court Street, Suite 111, 1st Floor. Phone 515-993-5808, email propertytax@dallascountyiowa.gov. The directory lists Summer Portzen as treasurer.
  • Assessor: 515-993-5802. The directory lists Kelsey Straub and Steve Helm.
  • Auditor: 515-993-6914, which sets levy rates from local budgets.
  • Recorder: 800 Court Street, Suite 130. Phone 515-993-5804, open Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., and it has an online record search and a transfer tax calculator.

When are Dallas County property taxes due?

The first half is due September 1 and goes delinquent after September 30. The second half is due March 1 and goes delinquent after March 31. Statements are mailed in August.

Late interest is 1.5 percent per month, rounded to the nearest dollar. Dallas County accepts only the U.S. Postal Service postmark as proof of mailing, and it does not accept check dates or business meter dates. The treasurer suggests asking the post office to postmark the envelope while you wait.

Not receiving a statement does not excuse a payment. New owners should call for one, and owners with a mortgage lender should check that the lender has the correct parcel data.

What is the Dallas County tax sale?

The annual tax sale is held on the third Monday in June, and the treasurer can pick a different date if needed. The treasurer runs the sale, processes redemptions, issues tax sale deeds and handles suspensions.

A certificate holder may pay later delinquent taxes after November 15 and May 15 if a half remains unpaid. Under the state's tax sale rules, owners and others with a recorded interest can redeem by paying the tax sold and 2 percent per month. An unredeemed lien can lead to a tax deed.

How are Dallas County assessments set and protested?

The assessor values each parcel as of January 1, and Iowa's cycle runs about 18 months to payment. A January 2026 assessment leads to bills in fall 2027 and spring 2028.

Protests go to the Board of Review between April 2 and April 30 under Iowa Code 441.37. Grounds include unequal treatment against like property, a value above the legal amount, exemption or misclassification, a mistake, or fraud. The board cannot extend the deadline, and in federal disaster counties the window can move to May 1 through June 5.

After a state equalization order, a second protest period runs October 9 to October 31, limited to arguing the order pushed value past what Iowa Code 441.21 allows. Appeals go to the Property Assessment Appeal Board or to district court within 20 days after the board adjourns.

What does the 2026 homestead change mean for a Dallas County seller?

Senate File 2472, signed May 18, 2026, replaces the old homestead tax credit with an exemption equal to 10 percent of taxable value, between $5,500 and $20,000, starting with the 2026 assessment year. It first shows up on the September 2027 and March 2028 bills.

The state says people already claiming the credit do not need to refile. The disabled veteran credit stays. The Department of Revenue's property tax division at 515-281-3114 answers eligibility questions.

What happens to taxes and recording when a Dallas County house sells?

The seller's share of the current year's tax is usually credited to the buyer at closing, and the deed is recorded in the Recorder's office in Adel.

Iowa charges 80 cents per $500 of value over the first $500 in transfer tax, and each deed needs a declaration of value signed by a seller, a buyer or an agent. The assessor holds the declaration for three years from December 31 of the transfer year. Which side pays the tax is set by the contract, since the statute does not say.

The first half is due September 1 and the second half is due March 1. Late interest of 1.5 percent per month applies after September 30 and March 31.

Where is the Dallas County Treasurer?

The tax division is at 800 Court Street, Suite 111, Adel, on the first floor of the Administration Building. The phone is 515-993-5808.

When is the Dallas County tax sale?

It is held on the third Monday in June unless the treasurer sets a different date.

How do I protest my Dallas County assessment?

File a written petition with the Board of Review between April 2 and April 30. If you disagree with the decision, appeal to the Property Assessment Appeal Board or to district court.

Do Dallas County owners need to refile for the new homestead exemption?

No. The Department of Revenue says current homestead credit claimants do not need to refile. New owners need to apply for their own.

Where is Buchanan County, Iowa, and how is it organized?

Buchanan County is in northeast Iowa, and Independence is both the county seat and its largest city. Wikipedia reports that the county was formed on December 21, 1837, from part of Dubuque County and named for James Buchanan, then a senator and later the 15th president.

The county covers 573 square miles, nearly all of it land, and is divided into sixteen townships. It borders Clayton, Fayette, Delaware, Linn, Benton, Black Hawk and Bremer counties. The 2020 census counted 20,565 residents, down slightly from 20,958 in 2010, and about 67 percent of people live in rural areas. That rural share means many Buchanan County parcels are acreage or farm sites, not town lots, and the tax bill follows the parcel.

Ten school districts reach into the county, including Independence, Jesup, Oelwein, Union, Vinton-Shellsburg and Wapsie Valley.

What is Independence, Iowa, known for?

Independence was founded June 15, 1847, and incorporated October 15, 1864. It took the county seat from Quasqueton, then a village of fewer than 15 residents. The county courthouse built in 1857 was replaced in 1939 by an Art Deco building.

In the late 1880s and early 1890s the town was a nationally known horse-racing center, nicknamed the "Lexington of the North." A written decision with reasons must come back from the board. If the board's answer does not satisfy you, an owner can go on to the Property Assessment Appeal Board or district court. Iowa charges a real estate transfer tax of 80 cents for each $500 of value above $500, and the seller is liable for it. The tax is paid to the county recorder, and a declaration of value must be filed when the deed is presented, or the recorder will refuse to record it.

Iowa Code section 428A.2 lists exemptions, including gifts between spouses or between parent and child, transfers to heirs without consideration and tax deeds. A sale to a buyer at full price is taxable. Of each month's receipts, 82.75 percent go to the Department of Revenue and the rest stays in the county general fund.

Where is Dubuque County and what is in it?

Dubuque County is in eastern Iowa, where the state meets Illinois and Wisconsin, and the Mississippi River forms its northeastern edge. The county seat and largest city is Dubuque. The 2020 census counted 99,266 residents, which made it the ninth most populous county in Iowa.

The county covers about 616 square miles. The east is hilly and wooded, part of the Driftless Area that glaciers skipped, while the west is mostly rolling farmland. Beyond Dubuque, the biggest communities in 2020 were Asbury (5,943 people), Dyersville (4,477), Cascade (2,386), Epworth (2,023), Peosta (1,908) and Farley (1,766).

The county was founded on October 1, 1834 and takes its name from Julien Dubuque, a French Canadian trader. The city of Dubuque was chartered a year earlier and is counted as the oldest city in Iowa. A house in a river bluff neighborhood and a house on a farm near Cascade can both be sold here, but they are taxed and assessed through the same county machinery, which is what this guide covers.

Who handles property tax in Dubuque County?

The Dubuque County Treasurer collects property tax, and the assessor's office for your parcel sets the value. The City of Dubuque states on its own site that it does not bill or collect property taxes. The county assesses and collects them, then passes the city's share along each month.

  • Treasurer: Michael Clasen, County Court House, 720 Central Avenue, Dubuque, IA 52001. The city's page lists office hours of 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday.
  • Courthouse main line: 563-589-1300, mailing address PO Box 5001, Dubuque, IA 52004-5001.
  • Appointments: the county website says the treasurer's office takes appointments that can be booked online to skip the line.
  • Property search: the county links a Beacon property records lookup from its home page.

Dubuque also has a city assessor. A 2020 presentation to the city council was given by Troy Patzner as Dubuque City Assessor, so a parcel inside city limits may be valued by that office rather than the county's. If you are unsure, call the courthouse and give the parcel number.

Courthouse address720 Central Avenue, Dubuque
Treasurer hours (city page)8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday to Friday

When are Dubuque County property taxes due?

Iowa property tax is paid in two halves, and the statewide calendar applies to Dubuque County. The first half is due September 1 and the second half March 1, with a grace period to the end of each month.

  • Statements go out in August after the county auditor certifies the levy.
  • September 30 is the first-half deadline, and March 31 is the second-half deadline. If either date lands on a weekend, it moves to the next business day.
  • Unpaid first-half tax is delinquent in October and unpaid second-half tax in April.
  • Interest on a delinquent installment runs 1.5 percent per month, with a one dollar minimum.

Iowa taxes run a year behind. The September and March payments cover the fiscal year that ended the previous June 30. That matters if you sell: you can owe tax for a period when the house was still yours even if the buyer takes over before the bill arrives.

A missing statement does not remove late charges. The state's treasurers' association says it is the owner's job to make sure a bill is received and paid, and you can pay with just the parcel number.

How does the Dubuque County tax sale work?

Dubuque County holds a yearly online tax sale for parcels with unpaid tax, usually on the third Monday of June. The 2026 sale was set for Monday, June 15, 2026, with bidding open from 9:00 to 11:00 a.m. at iowataxauction.com. Bidders had to register by June 11.

The scale is worth seeing. The county's 2025 publication notice, for a June 16, 2025 sale, listed roughly 450 real estate parcels and about 130 mobile homes. Real estate amounts on that list ran from $6 to $104,077, including penalty and costs.

  • Redemption interest is 2 percent per month on the sale amount, and any part of a month counts as a full month.
  • On a regular sale, a 90-day notice of right of redemption may be issued after one year and nine months from the sale date.
  • On a public bidder sale, the 90-day notice may go out nine months after the sale.
  • A redemption only counts if the treasurer receives it before close of business on the 90th day after service is complete.

A property marked with an asterisk in the notice has been advertised for two years without a sale. If no private bid arrives, the county itself bids the amount due. Anyone holding such a parcel and thinking of selling should talk to the treasurer before the next June sale.

How are Dubuque homes valued, and how do you appeal?

Iowa assessors value residential property at 100 percent of market value, then a state rollback percentage cuts that to a taxable value. Dubuque's own assessor explained the method in 2020: sales of similar homes, replacement cost less depreciation, and for rentals an income approach.

Real property is reassessed every two years, in odd-numbered years. The Department of Revenue checks assessments against actual sales, and if a class falls outside a 95 to 105 percent ratio band it can order an adjustment. In Dubuque's 2019 cycle the residential rollback was 55.0743 percent. Rollbacks change every year, and a 2025 example from the Iowa Taxpayers Research foundation used 44.5345 percent for residential property. Statewide taxable growth for existing homes is capped at 3 percent.

To contest a value, you file a written protest with the local Board of Review between April 2 and April 30 of the assessment year. Iowa Code 441.37 allows five grounds:

  • the assessment is not equitable compared with similar property;
  • it is above the value the law allows;
  • the property is misclassified or should be exempt;
  • there is an error in the assessment;
  • there was fraud or misconduct, which must be stated specifically.

A hearing can be requested in writing when you file. The board must send a written decision with its reasons. If you disagree, the next step is the Property Assessment Appeal Board or district court, and the PAAB can be reached at 515-725-0338.

What does the Dubuque economy mean for a seller?

Dubuque's employer base is broad, which keeps a steady pool of local buyers and renters. The city's largest employers include John Deere (about 2,600 people), the Dubuque Community School District (about 1,957), MercyOne Dubuque Medical Center (about 1,410) and Medical Associates (about 1,061). Finley Hospital, Andersen Windows and Doors, Sedgwick Claims Management Services and Medline Industries are also major names.

Manufacturing was the base until the 1980s farm crisis, when unemployment in the county hit 23 percent in one month of 1982. The economy has since added health care, finance, education and tourism, and the city draws more than 2 million visitors a year to the Port of Dubuque and its riverfront.

Five colleges are in the city: Loras, Clarke, the University of Dubuque, Emmaus University and a Northeast Iowa Community College campus presence, with the largest NICC campus in nearby Peosta. Anyone selling near a campus or in the older parts of the city should expect buyers to compare the house with its neighbors on age and condition.

What property conditions affect a Dubuque County sale?

Hills, river flooding and age are the three physical issues buyers ask about first. The city sits among bluffs in the Driftless Area, so slope matters when a buyer looks at a lot. Lower areas by the river and creeks carry flood risk, and the city has worked on the North End by opening up parts of Bee Branch Creek in 2015 and 2016. Flash flooding in places such as Valley View is still being dealt with.

Dubuque's neighborhoods have different building eras. The downtown area includes the Fenelon Place Residential Historic District, the North End grew with German settlers, the South End is historically Irish American, and the West End grew after World War II. A 2020 housing count found 27,174 units in the city, with a 1.5 percent homeowner vacancy rate.

Older houses in any of these areas often need roofs, wiring, foundation work or sewer line repairs before a traditional buyer's inspector signs off. A cash sale as-is avoids that repair list, though you should still confirm taxes and any special assessments with the treasurer first.

How are property taxes handled when you sell a Dubuque County house?

Taxes are normally prorated on the closing statement, with the buyer credited for the seller's share or the seller paying the treasurer directly. The state's treasurers' site adds that a seller closing between July 1 and December 31 owes the September installment, and a seller closing between January 1 and June 30 owes the March installment.

  • Delinquent tax and tax sale amounts must be paid in full before a clean transfer.
  • Every deed that conveys Iowa real estate for more than $500 carries state transfer tax of 80 cents per $500 or fraction above $500 (Iowa Code 428A.1).
  • A declaration of value, signed by a buyer or seller, goes to the county recorder with the deed. The recorder sends it to the assessor, who keeps it for three years.

Because the assessor receives those declarations, your sale price can become evidence in later valuation work. That is one reason to keep the settlement statement.

You pay the Dubuque County Treasurer at the courthouse, 720 Central Avenue in Dubuque, or by calling the courthouse for current payment options. The City of Dubuque does not collect property tax.

What happens if I miss the September 30 payment in Dubuque County?

The first half becomes delinquent in October and interest of 1.5 percent per month is added, with a one dollar minimum. If it stays unpaid, the parcel can be listed for the June tax sale.

Can I sell a Dubuque County house that is in the tax sale list?

Yes, but the delinquent tax, penalty and costs have to be paid, usually from the sale proceeds at closing. Once a certificate is sold, redemption also carries 2 percent interest per month on the sale amount.

When can I protest my Dubuque County assessment?

Written protests go to the Board of Review between April 2 and April 30 of the assessment year. Outside that window, only clerical or mathematical errors can be corrected.

Where is Monona County, Iowa, and how big is it?

Monona County is a western Iowa county on the Missouri River that covers 699 square miles, 694 of them land. The 2020 census counted 8,751 residents, about 12.5 people per square mile, and the county seat and largest city is Onawa.

It borders Woodbury County to the north, Crawford to the east and Harrison to the south, while Burt and Thurston counties in Nebraska lie across the river to the west and southwest. With that density, a typical sale here is a small-town house or a rural parcel with more land than neighbors.

How has Monona County's population changed over time?

The county peaked at about 17,980 people around 1900 and has been falling since 1940. The 2025 estimate is 8,539, roughly half the peak.

Monona County was formed in 1851 and organized in 1854. The seat moved from Ashton to Onawa in 1858, when the first courthouse was completed. Lewis and Clark stopped in the area in 1804, and the spot is now Lewis and Clark State Park. From 1900 to 2004 the county was a national political bellwether, a status that no longer applies.

With a population that has fallen for generations, sellers should price from nearby recorded sales rather than from replacement cost.

What is Onawa known for, and why does the setting matter to owners?

Onawa was platted in 1857, got its railway in 1867 and is described as the largest town on the Iowa side of the Missouri River between Council Bluffs and Sioux City. It is also known for having the widest main street in the continental United States.

The town lies in the Loess Hills, a band of wind-deposited silt roughly 200 miles long that runs along the Missouri River. The soil, called sugar clay, hardens when dry but loses its cohesion when wet, which causes slumping on slopes. The West Monona Community School District serves Onawa.

  • Loess Hills State Forest covers 10,600 acres across Harrison and Monona counties.
  • Preparation Canyon State Park, 344 acres, sits near Pisgah.
  • Lewis and Clark State Park marks the area Lewis and Clark passed in 1804.

If your lot is on a slope or near a cut bank, expect a buyer's inspector to look at drainage and foundation movement.

Does Missouri River flooding affect Monona County sellers?

It can, because the county borders the river and floods there have lasted a long time. During the 2019 floods, Missouri River flooding in some places ran as long as seven months, and the I-29 corridor in western Iowa was closed in several stretches, according to Wikipedia's summary of the 2019 Midwestern floods.

That summary describes the hardest-hit area as the valley south of Council Bluffs, not Monona County. Still, a seller on or near the floodplain should have flood insurance history and any repair records ready.

State rules also account for disasters. When a county is declared a disaster area after March 1 and before May 20, the property protest deadline moves from April 30 to June 5, and the board of review can sit until June 15.

How are Monona County properties valued?

All real property is reassessed every two years, in odd-numbered years, with a January 1 effective date. The assessor places each parcel in one of five classes: residential, multi-residential, commercial, industrial or agricultural.

Farmland is valued by productivity and earning capacity rather than market value, though farm dwellings are not valued that way. In a county with 694 square miles of land, a farm seller should know which part of the property is the dwelling and which is land, since the two are valued differently.

What are the Monona County protest steps and dates?

Ask for an informal review from April 2 to April 25, or file a written protest by April 30. The board of review then meets from May 1 until it adjourns.

  • April 2 to 30: written protest to the board of review.
  • May 1 onward: board hears protests, with a limit of May 31 unless extended.
  • October 9 to 31 of odd years: protest for properties hit by a state equalization order.

The board can confirm, raise or lower an assessment, and its decision can be appealed to the Property Assessment Appeal Board or district court within 20 days of adjournment or May 31, whichever is later. Grounds are set in Iowa Code 441.37, and the protest has to be in writing.

What are the late-payment and tax sale rules for Monona County?

Delinquent installments grow by one and one-half percent for every month, rounded to the nearest dollar, until paid. Tax is paid in halves, and the statute treats the first half as delinquent from October 1 and the second from April 1.

Unpaid parcels go to a public sale on the third Monday of June under Iowa Code 446.7. After a sale, the owner can still pay the sale amount plus 2% a month to redeem, as section 447.1 sets out. Monona's Treasurer page lists a Tax Sale section but did not show details when we reviewed it, so call the office for current dates.

The deed goes to the recorder with a declaration of value, and Iowa transfer tax runs 80 cents for each $500 over the first $500 (Iowa Code 428A.1). The recorder sends the declaration to the assessor, who holds it three years.

The homestead credit asks an owner to occupy the home on July 1 and for at least six months of the year. If a house sells before July 1, the buyer must apply by July 1. A sale after that date leaves the credit with the property for that year (rule 701-110.1).

Mahaska County was formed in 1843, named for Chief Mahaska of the Iowa people, and began governing itself in 1844. Coal mining was once a leading industry, and by 1895 the county out-produced every other Iowa county in coal.

The Muchakinock coal camp near Oskaloosa was among the largest in Iowa in the 1800s, and a 1902 explosion at the Lost Creek No. 2 mine killed 20 men. Oskaloosa was platted and named county seat in 1844 and incorporated in 1875. Its courthouse, finished in 1886 and designed by Henry C. Koch, is on the National Register of Historic Places.

William Penn University was founded by Quakers in 1873 as Penn College, took the William Penn College name in 1933 and became a university in 2000. The headcounts in that survey date from 2010, so treat them as background only.

Forms exist for residential, commercial and agricultural property. The Assessor says commercial owners may offer three years of operating statements and a current rent roll, though that is not required. Grounds follow Iowa Code 441.37, and the details are in the Assessor summary.

Where is Madison County, Iowa, and which towns are in it?

Madison County sits in south-central Iowa, covers about 562 square miles, and counted 16,548 residents in the 2020 census. Winterset is both the county seat and the largest city.

The county touches Dallas, Warren, Clarke, Union and Adair counties, and it meets Polk County at a single corner point. What is the history behind Madison County?

Madison County was formed on January 13, 1846, and began governing itself in 1849. It carries the name of President James Madison, and Hiram Hurst is credited as the first European-American settler, arriving from Missouri around April 1846.

Winterset itself was platted in the summer of 1849. Its planned name was Summerset, but the commissioners switched it to Winterset after a stretch of unseasonably cold weather. The county courthouse there went up in 1868 and was rebuilt in 1876 after a fire.

Six of the county's original sixteen covered bridges still stand. The Roseman Covered Bridge appeared in the 1995 film The Bridges of Madison County, and the Holliwell Bridge did too. Winterset also holds the Covered Bridge Festival every second weekend in October, and the John Wayne Birthplace Museum opened there in 2015.

The most serious recent weather event in the county was a low-end EF4 tornado on March 5, 2022, which struck just outside Winterset and killed six people. Sellers with storm or hail damage should keep roofing and repair records, because buyers and lenders will ask for them.

You can file a written protest from April 2 through April 30 of the assessment year. Notices go out around April 1, and the Assessor's calendar also offers an informal review from April 2 to April 25 before you decide to file.

If you want an oral hearing, ask for it in writing when you file. A county placed under a disaster declaration can see the filing period move to May 1 through June 5.

Who sits on the Madison County Board of Review?

The Madison County Board of Review has three members: a farmer, a licensed real estate broker and a contractor, all from the county. The conference board appoints them, and the Assessor's office does not control their decisions.

The board meets from May 1 until it finishes, and state rules call for adjournment by May 31 unless the Department of Revenue extends the session. It sends a written decision with reasons. If you disagree, the next step is the Property Assessment Appeal Board or district court, with a 20 day clock that starts at adjournment or May 31, whichever is later, according to the Department of Revenue's board of review summary.

How do you pay Madison County property tax, and when is it late?

Iowa lets you pay the full year or two halves, and a half that is unpaid goes delinquent on October 1 or April 1. After that, interest runs at one and one-half percent a month, rounded to the nearest dollar with a $1 minimum, and any part of a month counts as a whole one (Iowa Code 445.39).

The county Treasurer takes payment at the annex, by mail with a check payable to the Treasurer, or online. The Treasurer's site says 2026/2027 statements are available. A delinquency notice goes out if the first half is unpaid by February 1, and not receiving it does not excuse the payment, per the older Iowa Code chapter 445 text.

The treasurer must offer parcels with delinquent taxes at the annual tax sale, held on the third Monday in June unless there is good cause for another June date (Iowa Code 446.7). Each parcel sells for the taxes, interest, fees and costs owed.

The original owner can still redeem after the sale. The redemption amount includes the sale price, a certificate fee and interest at two percent a month counted from the month of sale, under Iowa Code 447.1. Interest is costly, so settling the balance before June is the cheaper path.

Iowa also charges a real estate transfer tax of 80 cents for each $500 of value above the first $500, as set out in Iowa Code 428A.1. The statute section does not say which side pays, so your purchase contract decides that.

Every two years, with a January 1 effective date, according to the county Assessor. Owners are asked to report new construction, remodels, finished basements, decks and any buildings removed or damaged.

Interest starts at one and one-half percent a month after the October 1 or April 1 delinquency date. A parcel still unpaid can be offered at the June tax sale.

How did Fort Dodge begin?

Fort Dodge began as an army post. On August 2, 1850, Captain Samuel Woods and Company E of the 6th Infantry arrived to build a fort where Lizard Creek meets the Des Moines River.

The post was first called Fort Clarke and then renamed for Henry Dodge, a former governor of Wisconsin Territory. The army left in 1853, a storekeeper named William Williams bought the land and buildings the next year, and the town was incorporated in 1869.

In 1872 the Fort Dodge Plaster Mills opened a gypsum mill, described as the first west of the Mississippi River. Gypsum from the area was used for the Cardiff Giant hoax, and a replica is on display at the Fort Museum and Frontier Village.

Meatpacking was a leading industry for most of the 20th century, and the last two large plants, owned by Iowa Beef Processors and Hormel, closed in the 1980s. Iowa Central Community College has its central campus in Fort Dodge.

Average precipitation is 35.09 inches a year and average snowfall is 39.0 inches. The record low is minus 35 degrees F and the record high is 110 degrees F.

US 20 crosses the middle of the county and bypasses Fort Dodge to the south, while US 169 passes on the west side and runs south to Harcourt. Iowa 7 ends at the northwest edge of the city, and Iowa 175 and Iowa 144 serve the southeast and south.

Fort Dodge Regional Airport, just north of the city, is mainly a general aviation field with daily flights to St. Louis and Minneapolis-St. Paul. DART runs six local bus routes on weekdays.

School districts in the county include Fort Dodge, Webster City, Eagle Grove, Gilmore City-Bradgate, Humboldt, Manson Northwest Webster, Stratford and Southeast Valley, which formed in 2023 from a merger.

Webster County revalues real property every two years, in odd-numbered years, with an effective date of January 1. Market value is an estimate of what the property would sell for on that date.

A decision can be appealed to the Property Assessment Appeal Board or the district court within 20 days after the Board adjourns, or by May 31, whichever is later.

Iowa taxes are paid in two halves, due September 1 and March 1, with late interest of 1.5 percent a month starting October 1 and April 1. In a sale, taxes are usually prorated and the buyer is credited with the seller's share.

Unpaid taxes can go to tax sale. The owner can redeem by paying the sale amount plus 2 percent a month and fees of $20 each for the certificate and redemption, and a tax sale deed can follow if the redemption period passes.

Appraisers cite Iowa Code section 441.17 for the right to enter property for assessment. They knock before exterior work, leave if you ask, and need your permission for interior walk-throughs of new construction.

When are Carroll County property taxes due, and what happens if they are late?

Iowa property tax is paid in two halves, with the first half due September 1 and the second half due March 1. Interest starts the next month, October 1 for the first half and April 1 for the second, at 1.5 percent per month, with weekend rules that can move the cutoff a day or two.

Under Iowa Code 445.37, a payment that is not made electronically has to reach the treasurer by the last business day before the delinquent month, or be postmarked in time. Statements go to the titleholder of record even when a mortgage lender pays from escrow.

How does the Carroll County tax sale work?

Carroll County sells unpaid taxes once a year, on the third Monday in June, and the 2026 sale ran on June 15 online through GovEase, with bidding from 9:00 to 10:30 a.m. Bidders had to register between May 18 and June 11 and pay a $40 registration fee.

Bidding starts at 100 percent and moves down in whole percentages. The lowest percentage wins, and ties go to a random draw. The winner pays the delinquent taxes, interest and a $20 certificate fee, and the owner keeps the right to redeem by paying the sale amount plus 2 percent per month.

  • On a public bidder parcel, advertised for two years, the notice can be served after nine months.
  • The redemption amount can include a record search cost of up to $300, plus service and publication costs.
  • The delinquent list is published in the Carroll Times Herald in late May.

How do you protest a Carroll County assessment?

File a written petition with the Board of Review between April 2 and April 30 of the assessment year. The existing county listing says the same, and the board cannot extend the window.

The grounds under Iowa Code 441.37 are that the assessment is not equitable compared with like property, that it exceeds the legal value, that the property is exempt or misclassified, that there is an error, or that there is fraud. Petition forms are available from the assessor's office, and the Property Assessment Appeal Board explains the process on its own site.

In years when the state issues an equalization order that raises your class, a second short protest window runs from October 9 to October 31, and the only argument allowed is that the order pushed your value above what Iowa Code 441.21 permits. A decision can be appealed to the Property Assessment Appeal Board or to district court within 20 days after the board adjourns.

What does the new Iowa homestead exemption mean for a Carroll County seller?

Iowa replaced the homestead tax credit with a homestead exemption under SF 2472, signed May 18, 2026, and it applies from assessment year 2026. The exemption is 10 percent of the home's taxable value, with a floor of $5,500 and a ceiling of $20,000 of taxable value, and it first reaches bills paid in September 2027 and March 2028.

The Department of Revenue says current claimants do not need to refile.

What city incentives affect the value of a Carroll house?

The city of Carroll runs an urban revitalization area that offers a five year exemption on the first $75,000 of added value from improvements. Construction has to follow February 25, 2019 in the original area, or November 22, 2021 in the expanded area, and the project must raise assessed value by at least 10 percent.

The city also lists an Infill Housing Incentive of $20,000 per new owner-occupied home while funds last, and a speculative home loan program backed by five local banks. These programs favor new construction, so an older house competes with new homes that carry abatements and incentive money.

What happens to property tax when you sell a Carroll County house?

In a normal sale, the seller's share of the current tax is credited to the buyer at closing. The Iowa Treasurers' site says taxes are prorated and that the closing statement shows the split.

Iowa also charges a transfer tax of 80 cents for each $500 of value above the first $500, under Iowa Code 428A.1. A declaration of value, signed by at least one seller or buyer, goes in with every deed, and the recorder forwards it to the assessor, who keeps it three years. The statute does not say which party pays the tax, so the purchase contract decides that.

Unpaid city charges such as water or sewer that have been certified to the treasurer become a lien with the same priority as ordinary tax. They have to be cleared at closing.

The first half is due September 1 and the second half is due March 1. Interest begins October 1 and April 1 at 1.5 percent per month, and weekend dates can shift the cutoff.

Where do I pay Carroll County property tax?

Pay at the Carroll County Treasurer on the first floor of the courthouse, 114 E. 6th Street, Carroll, or call 712-792-1200. The Iowa Treasurers' site also takes online payments, with a fee for cards and e-checks.

When can I protest my Carroll County assessment?

You can file between April 2 and April 30 of the assessment year with the Board of Review. A second window from October 9 to October 31 applies only when a state equalization order raises your value.

Will my Carroll County property tax change after the reappraisal?

It can. New values take effect January 1, 2027, and the assessor expects them to apply to taxes payable in fiscal 2028 and 2029. Notices come after January 1, 2027.

Can I sell a Carroll County house that has back taxes?

Yes. Back taxes and interest are paid from the sale proceeds at closing. If the taxes have already been sold at the June tax sale, the redemption amount, which includes 2 percent per month, has to be paid too.

Where is Fayette County, Iowa, and how is it laid out?

Fayette County is in northeastern Iowa, with West Union as the county seat and Oelwein as the largest city. It covers about 731 square miles, almost all of it land, and is divided into 20 townships. Neighbors include Allamakee, Winneshiek, Clayton, Delaware, Buchanan, Bremer, Chickasaw and Black Hawk counties.

The 2020 census counted 19,509 people, and about 70 percent lived in rural areas. The county has lost residents steadily since it peaked at 29,845 in 1900. Of 9,298 housing units in 2020, 76.1 percent were owner-occupied.

The larger communities in 2020 were Oelwein (5,920), West Union (2,490), Sumner (2,030, mostly in Bremer County), Fayette (1,256), Fairbank (1,111), Elgin (685) and Clermont (586). Several of these sit across county lines, so a house with a Sumner or Fairbank mailing address may be billed by a different county than you expect. Check the parcel record before you look for a tax bill.

What is the history behind Fayette County and its towns?

Fayette County was created on December 21, 1837, while the region was part of Wisconsin Territory, and it was organized in 1850. It was named for the Marquis de Lafayette, the French general of the American Revolution. The city of Fayette carries the same name.

Oelwein grew because of the railroad. The town was laid out in 1872 on land bought from settler Gustav Oelwein. In the 1890s the Chicago Great Western Railway chose it as a center, and its locomotive and car repair shops opened in May 1899, which earned the town the nicknames Shop City and Hub City. Most tracks in several directions were pulled out in the early 1980s.

Two disasters shaped the main street area. An 1887 fire destroyed most of the old business district, and a 1968 tornado destroyed 68 homes and 51 businesses. Houses in town today sit on lots that were rebuilt in those periods, so age and condition vary a good deal from block to block.

What drives the Fayette County economy?

The county economy is small-town and mixed, with rail repair, schools, a college and farming as the visible anchors. In Oelwein, Transco Railway Products employs about 190 people repairing railroad cars, a direct descendant of the old shop-town trade. The Hub City Heritage Museum at 26 2nd Avenue SW keeps that history on display.

Fayette, on the Volga River, is home to Upper Iowa University, a private college founded in 1857. The city's median age in 2020 was 24.0, far below the county's 44.0, so rentals and student housing are part of the picture there. Oelwein sits at the junction of Iowa Highways 3 and 150.

  • Median age in the county, 2020: 44.0
  • Population change 2010 to 2020: down 6.6 percent
  • 2025 population estimate: 19,047

A shrinking county with older owners means more inherited and vacant houses. Sellers in that position often need to clear tax, title and condition questions at once, which is where the county offices below come in.

Who handles property tax in Fayette County?

The county's Beacon online mapping site lets you look up property valuations. The treasurer's page says statements are mailed once a year, usually in the first week of August, and the amount depends on assessed values and the budgets of schools, cities, the county, townships and community colleges.

When are Fayette County taxes due, and what does the assessor calendar look like?

Fayette County taxes are split into two equal installments, payable on or before September 30 and March 31. The county assessor's page lays out the rest of the year.

  • January 1: assessment date. Owners are notified by April 1.
  • April 2 to April 25: ask the assessor for an informal review of your value.
  • April 2 to April 30: file a written protest with the Board of Review.
  • May 1: the board begins meeting. It hears appeals through May 31, and the Director of Revenue can extend that to July 15.
  • July 1: filing deadline for the homestead credit, disabled veteran homestead credit and military exemption.
  • October 16 to 25: protests of the final equalization order.

The assessor says real property is revalued every two years. Owners are also expected to report new buildings, decks, garages, additions and demolished structures. The page warns that failing to report can bring a 100 percent valuation penalty under Iowa Code 441.24, so a seller who added a garage without telling the assessor should know about that before listing.

How is the Fayette County Board of Review set up?

The Board of Review has three or five members who serve staggered six-year terms, appointed by the Conference Board. The Conference Board is made up of the Board of Supervisors, the mayors of the cities and a representative from each school district.

Membership has to include a farmer, a real estate sales representative and someone from architecture or construction, and no more than two members may share an occupation. The same Conference Board appoints the assessor to a six-year term.

A protest must be in writing on the state form and rest on one of five grounds in Iowa Code 441.37, including inequity compared to similar property, a value above what the law allows, misclassification, an error, or fraud. A hearing can be requested when you file. The board has to give a written decision with its reasons.

What changes in Iowa's homestead rules affect Fayette County sellers?

Iowa is replacing the homestead credit with a homestead exemption. The Department of Revenue says the exemption is 10 percent of the homestead's taxable value, with a floor of $5,500 and a cap of $20,000 in taxable value. It applies from assessment year 2026, with the first benefit showing in taxes paid in September 2027 and March 2028.

The old credit equaled the tax on $4,850 of value. People already receiving it do not need to refile, and the disabled veteran homestead credit is kept. A buyer who takes over a Fayette County house will need to claim the exemption for themselves, and the assessor's July 1 deadline applies to that claim. Seller and buyer should ask the assessor how the claim is handled for a sale that closes close to that date.

How are taxes handled when you sell a Fayette County house?

Taxes on a Fayette County sale are normally prorated at closing, and any delinquent amount has to be cleared first. Iowa taxes lag a year, so the bill covers the fiscal year ending the previous June 30.

  • The state transfer tax is 80 cents per $500 of value above $500 (Iowa Code 428A.1), and a declaration of value is filed with the county recorder.

If the tax stays unpaid, the parcel can go to the county tax sale, held on the third Monday of June unless the treasurer sets another date. The Fayette County treasurer page does not describe tax sales, so call 563-422-3787 for the current notice list.

They are due in two equal installments, payable on or before September 30 and March 31. Statements are mailed in the first week of August.

You file in writing with the county Board of Review between April 2 and April 30. You can ask the assessor for an informal review from April 2 to April 25 first.

No. The assessor states that real property is revalued every two years, with a January 1 assessment date and notices out by April 1.

Yes. Taxes owed are usually settled from the proceeds at closing, and delinquent amounts must be paid before a clean transfer. Call the treasurer for a payoff figure.

Where is Hancock County, Iowa, and what towns does it include?

Hancock County is in north-central Iowa, bordered by Winnebago County to the north, Cerro Gordo to the east, Wright to the south and Kossuth to the west. Garner is the county seat. The county covers about 573 square miles and had 10,795 residents in the 2020 census.

How did Hancock County and Garner get started?

Hancock County was founded on January 15, 1851 and named for John Hancock of the Continental Congress. An election on June 28, 1858 established it fully, and the county seat moved to Garner from Concord, about a mile south, when the courthouse cornerstone was laid on June 8, 1899.

Garner was platted by the Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul Railroad in 1870 and incorporated on November 19, 1881. It was named for a railroad engineer, Col. W. W. Garner. Forest City was once called Puckerbrush. It was officially founded in 1855, platted in 1856 and incorporated June 14, 1878, after local leaders persuaded the Minneapolis and St. Louis Railroad to route through it. Swedish and Norwegian settlers came to a landscape that looked like home.

What jobs and employers shape the Hancock County housing market?

Manufacturing and education are the named employers in the county's two largest towns. Forest City is where Winnebago Industries, the motorhome maker, began in 1960 when investors took over a failing travel trailer factory. The company announced in August 2021 that it would move its corporate headquarters to Eden Prairie, Minnesota, but keep manufacturing in Forest City.

Waldorf University, a private four-year school, is also in Forest City, and the Forest City Community School District runs a wind turbine that supplies about 60 percent of its schools' energy needs.

In Garner, Stellar Industries and Iowa Mold Tooling Company make truck-mounted equipment such as service cranes and mechanics trucks. The county's school districts include Garner-Hayfield-Ventura (formed July 1, 2015), Forest City, West Hancock, Belmond-Klemme and West Fork, along with Algona and Clarion-Goldfield-Dows.

A county with a falling and aging population has a steady supply of older houses coming up for sale. Owners of those houses often find that repairs and unpaid taxes both need attention before a conventional listing works.

What does the north-central Iowa climate mean for a Hancock County house?

Forest City's climate is classed as hot-summer humid continental, with about 35.92 inches of precipitation and 40.2 inches of snow in an average year. Recorded extremes there run from 108 degrees Fahrenheit in July to minus 36 in winter.

For a seller, that range explains the usual inspection list on older rural and small-town houses: roof condition, insulation, heating equipment and basement moisture. Buyers who finance often need these items fixed or priced in. An as-is cash buyer can skip the repair step, though any lien, back tax or open permit still has to be cleared at closing.

How do Hancock County assessment appeals work?

A Hancock County owner who disagrees with a valuation files a written protest with the Board of Review between April 2 and April 30. The Hancock board has five members and meets on or about May 1.

The protest has to name one of the grounds in Iowa Code 441.37: the value is inequitable compared with similar property, it exceeds what the law allows, the property is misclassified or exempt, there is an error, or there was fraud. The board must send a written decision with its reasons.

Iowa residential rollback is a state number, set each year to keep taxable growth to 3 percent across the state. A 2025 example from the Iowa Taxpayers Research foundation used a residential rollback of 44.5345 percent. Rollback does not cap local levy rates, so a bill can still rise.

Iowa is also replacing the homestead credit with a homestead exemption of 10 percent of taxable value, with a minimum of $5,500 and a maximum of $20,000, starting with assessment year 2026.

How does the Hancock County tax sale work?

  • Notice of the sale must be mailed by May 1 to the name the parcel is taxed under.
  • Redeeming a parcel needs guaranteed funds and carries 2 percent interest per month.

An owner who has fallen behind on a Hancock County house should not wait for the June list. Selling before the sale lets the taxes be paid from proceeds rather than redeemed at 2 percent a month.

What happens to property tax when you sell in Hancock County?

Taxes are prorated at closing or paid by the seller to the treasurer directly, and they always run a year behind. A sale between July 1 and December 31 leaves the seller owing the September installment, while a sale from January 1 to June 30 leaves the March one.

Iowa's state transfer tax is 80 cents for each $500 of value above $500 (Iowa Code 428A.1). A declaration of value is submitted to the county recorder with the deed. The recorder forwards it to the assessor, who keeps it for three years from December 31 of the transfer year.

Late interest is 1.5 percent per month and begins the first day after the installment goes delinquent. A missing statement does not waive it, since the state says the owner is responsible for making sure a bill is received.

Redemption needs guaranteed funds and carries 2 percent interest per month on top of the amount the parcel sold for. Ask the treasurer for an exact payoff.

Partly. Forest City lies in both Hancock and Winnebago counties, so the county where the parcel sits determines which treasurer bills the tax.

Where is Cass County, Iowa?

Cass County is in southwest Iowa, about 565 square miles, with Atlantic as the county seat. It borders Audubon County to the north, Adair to the east, Adams to the southeast, Montgomery to the southwest, Pottawattamie to the west and Shelby to the northwest.

The county is split into sixteen townships. Atlantic is by far the largest place, with 6,792 people in 2020. Griswold (994), Anita (963), Massena (359), Lewis (357), Cumberland (251), Marne (110) and Wiota (91) make up most of the rest of the towns.

Sellers in the smaller towns and on rural parcels deal with the same county offices as sellers in Atlantic, but the rural parcels also carry the rural services levy discussed below.

What is the history of Cass County?

Cass County was named for Lewis Cass, a Michigan senator and the 1848 Democratic nominee for president, and it took its present shape in 1851. Mormons leaving Illinois founded the first community, Indiantown, in 1846.

The county seat started at Lewis and moved to Atlantic after a vote declared on October 20, 1869. Courthouse fires have shaped the town square: the second courthouse, built in the 1880s, burned in 1932, and the fourth and current building was finished in 1934.

The county's population hit a high of 21,274 in 1900. Since then it has fallen in nearly every census, to 13,127 in 2020, with an estimate of 12,960 for 2025.

What does Atlantic offer in roads, rail and jobs?

Atlantic sits on the East Nishnabotna River, with Interstate 80 about 7 to 10 miles to the north and three exits serving the city. US-6 runs east and west through downtown toward Council Bluffs and Des Moines, and US-71 turns south at the edge of town.

Freight still moves on the Iowa Interstate Railroad, the successor to the Rock Island, whose 1898 depot now holds the Chamber of Commerce offices. Passenger trains stopped in 1970. The nearest Amtrak stops are Omaha and Creston, each about 58 miles away.

The Atlantic Coca-Cola Bottling Company has operated since 1929 and distributes across Iowa and parts of four neighboring states. The city's daily paper is the Atlantic News-Telegraph. Schools are run by the Atlantic Community School District.

What do the Census Bureau figures say about Cass County housing?

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts for 2020 to 2024 show a median value of owner-occupied homes of $150,300 and an owner-occupied rate of 71.6 percent in Cass County. These are survey estimates, not appraisals of any one house.

Which Cass County offices handle property tax?

The assessor sets value, the auditor works out levy rates from local budgets, and the treasurer collects. All of the county offices are in the courthouse at 5 West 7th Street, Atlantic, IA 50022.

  • Board of Review: three or five members, independent of the assessor, who can confirm, raise or lower a value.

The treasurer's office also takes online payment through iowatreasurers.org, and it processes the property tax credit claims for seniors and disabled owners.

How does Cass County value a house?

Cass County assesses homes at 100 percent of market value as of January 1, and it reassesses real property every two years, in the odd numbered years. The assessor uses three approaches: comparable sales, replacement cost less depreciation plus land, and an income method for rental property.

Farmland is valued on its productivity and earning capacity, not on sale prices. New construction is valued by how finished it was on January 1.

The assessor does not collect tax, calculate the tax or set rates. What a home owes depends on its value relative to the total value in its taxing district.

When are Cass County property taxes due?

The first half of a Cass County bill is due September 1 and goes delinquent October 1. The second half is due March 1 and goes delinquent April 1.

Late interest is 1.5 percent a month, rounded to the nearest dollar, with a $1 minimum. A delinquent notice goes out to owners with unpaid taxes as of February 1, and a Delinquent Tax Statement and Tax Sale Notice follows in April. Taxes still unpaid on May 1 pick up a publication fee and are advertised for the June sale.

The Iowa Treasurers' FAQ adds that payment must be postmarked by the due date, that you do not need a statement to pay if you have the parcel number, and that partial payments are accepted if they exceed the interest and costs.

How does the Cass County tax sale work?

The annual Cass County tax sale takes place on the third Monday in June at 8:00 a.m., and adjourned sales follow on the third Monday of later months. Parcels advertised twice without a buyer go to a Public Bidder Sale, and the county must buy them if no private bidder steps forward.

Redemption costs 2 percent per month from the sale, and the office requires guaranteed funds for redemption payments. After the county receives a Certificate of Purchase, the treasurer may also file an ordinary lawsuit to collect.

Iowa treats sold taxes as paid and places a lien on the property. If the lien is not redeemed within the statutory period, the certificate holder can start tax deed proceedings, so an owner behind on taxes should deal with it well before a deed is possible.

How do you protest a Cass County assessment?

Protest to the Board of Review in writing during the spring window, then take any remaining dispute to the district court. The assessor's page lists two sets of dates, April 2 to April 30 in one place and April 7 to May 5 in another, and does not say which is current, so call the office to confirm.

State law, Iowa Code 441.37, sets April 2 through April 30. The board can be asked to review equity against similar property, the value, classification, errors or fraud. In odd numbered years, owners whose property was changed by a state equalization order have a separate protest period of October 16 to 25, according to the assessor.

The homestead credit and military exemption can be filed all year. Filing by July 1 applies to the current year and filing later applies the next year.

What should a Cass County seller know about taxes at closing?

At closing, the seller's part of the current year's tax is normally prorated and credited to the buyer. Iowa's treasurers say the closing statement shows the figures.

Iowa's transfer tax is 80 cents per $500 of value above the first $500, and a declaration of value goes in with the deed. The assessor keeps the declaration for three years. Unpaid sewer or water charges that the city certified to the treasurer become a lien with the same standing as taxes, and a mobile home needs a tax clearance form before it is moved.

A seller who lives outside Iowa after the sale may owe Iowa income tax on the gain, according to the Treasurers' FAQ, so check that before you close.

The first half is due September 1 and the second half is due March 1. Interest begins October 1 and April 1 at 1.5 percent per month.

The treasurer is in the Cass County Courthouse at 5 West 7th Street in Atlantic. The phone is 712-243-5503, and property tax services are open 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

When does Cass County hold its tax sale?

The annual sale is the third Monday in June at 8:00 a.m. Notices must be mailed by May 1, and adjourned sales follow monthly.

How often does Cass County reassess property?

Every two years, in the odd numbered years, with a January 1 effective date. Homes are valued at 100 percent of market value.

Can I sell a Cass County house with unpaid taxes?

Yes. Unpaid taxes and interest are paid out of the sale proceeds at closing. If the taxes were already sold, the redemption amount, which grows at 2 percent a month, is part of the payoff.

Where is Clayton County, Iowa, and what is the land like?

Clayton County is in the northeast corner of Iowa along the Mississippi River, and at roughly 792 square miles it is the fifth largest county in the state by area. Elkader is the county seat.

The county touches Allamakee, Winneshiek, Fayette, Buchanan, Delaware and Dubuque counties in Iowa, and across the river it faces Crawford and Grant counties in Wisconsin. It lies in the Driftless Area, which was missed by the last ice sheet, so streams have cut deep valleys and the Mississippi is edged with bluffs.

That terrain shapes real estate. A house on a ridge, in a river valley or on the flat land by the Mississippi has very different weather and flood exposure, even within a few miles.

What are the main towns in Clayton County?

Clayton County is almost entirely rural, with 99.1 percent of residents living in rural areas in 2020, and its towns are small. The 2020 census counted these places.

How did Clayton County begin?

Clayton County was formed on December 21, 1837, and named for John M. Clayton, a Delaware senator who later served as Secretary of State under Zachary Taylor.

Guttenberg on the river was the first county seat, from 1838 to 1843. German immigrants arrived there from 1845, and between 1845 and 1865 builders put up more than one hundred limestone buildings, many still standing in the Front Street Historic District. Elkader was platted and incorporated in 1846 and is named for the Algerian leader Emir Abdelkader.

Elkader's Keystone Bridge over the Turkey River, built of local sandstone, is described as the largest stone arch bridge west of the Mississippi.

What drives the Clayton County economy?

Farming, small manufacturing and meat processing carry most of the local economy. Postville is the clearest example: Agri Star Meat and Poultry employed about 700 people as of 2017, more than 30 percent of the town's population, and Norplex-Micarta has made laminated plastic products there since 1975.

Guttenberg began as a river trading town, with lead mining on Miners Creek and a flour mill. After the Civil War, railroads and an interior road system reduced its role as a regional market center.

Roads follow the same pattern. US 52 runs through Guttenberg, and Postville sits where US 18 and US 52 meet Iowa Highway 51. School districts include Central Community (Elkader), Clayton Ridge (Guttenberg and Garnavillo, merged in 2005), and Postville Community.

What weather and flood risks matter for a Clayton County house?

Clayton County has a documented flood record on two rivers. The National Weather Service lists record crests of 27.77 feet on the Turkey River at Elkader on June 10, 2008, where flood stage is 12 feet, and 23.65 feet on the Mississippi at Guttenberg on April 24, 1965, where flood stage is 15 feet.

June 2008 brought 3 to 7 inches of rain over two days, closed roads with mudslides and caused more than $10 million in property damage. Guttenberg's riverfront flooded many times, and a levee was built after 1965.

  • 14 documented tornadoes since 1950, including an F3 west of Elkader on May 30, 1985
  • 102 reports of large hail and 104 damaging wind reports since 1982

Clayton County assesses non-agricultural property at 100 percent of market value as of January 1, and the assessor must reassess everything in odd numbered years, with notices due by April 15.
